chapter: Failure in St. Louis and the Omaha bands
title: Jo Jones as teacher and why musicians hold jam sessions
summary: He contrasts Jo Jones, who liked teaching, with Lester Young, and says musicians held jam sessions because big bands gave few solos.

story.theme_name: Playing with Count Basie: joining, leading, leaving
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: Of course Joe Jones was a different sort of a person, a very -- an extrovert, Joe, a marvelous drummer. Was Joe a person that you related to let's say not exactly intellectually but -- well, I can better understand you and Lester be close than you and Joe.

Yes, well there again as I said, all of these people with talent, for some reason or other, always seeked out younger musicians or other musicians who had signs of either had talent or showed signs of talent. I'd have to say in this case I was a young fella who showed signs of promising some talent. I had -- I must have had some talent to show that I had promise of other talent. They were further advanced than I was, but my keen interest -- and as I said, which is important, I was always seeking to learn. And so naturally I admired these musicians and I put myself in the position whereas they respected my inquiry, and I was respectful of them, and I think that they learned to respect me and like me because I was interested.
And they felt that they could show me something.
Right. And so in other words as I said,

where these people would be hard to understand by others, who didn't fit in the environment or in this circle of musicians, well, I had no problems because they loved me. Well, now in the sense of the word. For instance I would have to say that Lester Young loved me because I later on played with them and he expressed his love for me warmly. Now, in the case of Jo Jones being another type of person, Jo Jones always was considered -- I think he considers himself and he acts in the form of a teacher. He always wanted to teach people, young guys. If he felt like he had an obligation. That's his personality.

And he still does. In other words, he enjoyed playing, and like, you know, when he played in a band, you're restricted to the four or five hours that you're playing a job, so -- and then you're restricted to a few solos. Now jazz music is based on solo work, ad lib, see. So -- all right, so you're just getting warmed up. So that's what caused this -- that's what brought about the jam sessions that I told you about before, because musicians want to play. And they don't get a chance to play enough in a big band where they've got 14 pieces, and guys singing and playing a little bit of this, and you've got to play music to people that want

to play it that you don't want to play, and you've got to play a part. We had just warmed up to play your instrument. Because you want to play, you want to experiment, you want to hear yourself playing, you want to get this feeling you will enjoy. And you're wide awake, you know, you're just ready to go when the dance is over, see.
And this is what Lester Young and the older musicians did. They'd go around and play with whoever -- whatever musicians they found in the town could play.
